data.claim: Blocking the three signals in the main thread and reading them with signal.sigtimedwait on a watcher thread yields si_pid/si_uid; /proc/<pid>/comm|status names the sender and its ancestry; a SIGUSR2 pthread_kill wakes the main thread so the existing RunTerminated path records the outcome; unblocking around Popen keeps the command's SigBlk clear.
data.falsifier: A helper process kills a running gate run with SIGTERM and the recorded evidence does not carry sender_pid == helper pid; or the run's child shows SIGTERM in SigBlk.
data.mechanism: A process-directed signal blocked in every thread stays pending and is consumed by sigtimedwait, which returns the full siginfo (Python handlers never see it). The signal mask is inherited across exec, so the spawn path must unblock for the child.

chunk_findings.detail: The `inherit_unblocked` helper reads blocked signals using `signal.pthread_sigmask(signal.SIG_BLOCK, [])`, but `pthread_sigmask` is only supported on the main thread in multi-threaded Python processes and raises a `ValueError` on secondary threads. While the function wraps the call in a `try...except (OSError, ValueError)` block, this means whenever `inherit_unblocked` is called from any worker thread (such as concurrent gate runner threads), `pthread_sigmask` will fail, catch the exception, and silently return the un-modified `kwargs`, failing to clear the signal mask for child processes spawned from those threads.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc.py:125

chunk_findings.detail: `inherit_unblocked` installs a Python-level `preexec_fn` whenever the spawning thread has `SIGTERM`, `SIGHUP`, or `SIGINT` blocked. The run owner is explicitly multithreaded (it uses a watcher thread to block signals and read sender information), so this makes `subprocess.run`/`Popen` fall back to fork and execute Python code in the child before `exec`. If another owner thread holds a lock at fork time (for example an allocator, import, logging, or interpreter-internal lock), the child can block inside the `functools.partial(signal.pthread_sigmask, ...)` call before it execs; the parent then waits forever on the child’s exec pipe, or a timeout becomes a spurious timeout. This is the documented `preexec_fn` multithreading hazard, and the new code applies it in exactly the threaded owner path (also used for the watcher spawn in `ddflow/adapters/proc_server.py`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc.py:inherit_unblocked

chunk_findings.detail: The guard `if "preexec_fn" in kwargs` treats an explicit `preexec_fn=None` as a caller-supplied hook and returns the kwargs unchanged. Given a thread with `SIGTERM` blocked and a call such as `proc.run(["sleep", "10"], preexec_fn=None)` (or a wrapper that passes `preexec_fn=None` to clear inherited settings), the child inherits the blocked `SIGTERM` mask; a later `kill(pid, SIGTERM)` does nothing until the child changes its own signal mask. `None` is subprocess’s “no preexec_fn” default, so it should not suppress the mask-clearing `preexec_fn`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/proc.py:inherit_unblocked

chunk_findings.detail: `with RUN.terminating(_record_kill_facts(bound.arguments)):` evaluates `_record_kill_facts` before `RUN.terminating.__enter__` can install the signal mask/watcher, and `_record_kill_facts` performs disk I/O via `Config.load(args["repo"])`. If a review has already called `_begin_run()` and a SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGINT arrives while `Config.load` is reading or stat-ing the repo config (slow NFS, locked file, permission check, etc.), the process is still using the default signal disposition, so the signal terminates the process instead of being converted into `RUN.RunTerminated`. `_terminated` then never runs, the forgotten prior runs are not replaced by a recorded outcome, and no `evidence.kill` is written. The knob should be resolved before the termination-critical section, or the signal mask should be installed before doing potentially slow config I/O.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:155

chunk_findings.detail: `_watching` starts a daemon watcher thread for the duration of the captured body, and this module states that `adapters.proc` clears child signal masks via `inherit_unblocked` used as a `preexec_fn`. In CPython, launching a subprocess with `preexec_fn` forks while other threads may be running; `preexec_fn` is explicitly not thread-safe and can deadlock if another thread holds an internal lock at fork time. Given `record_kill_facts` enabled, a gate run body that launches its command through `adapters.proc` is already multithreaded because the watcher thread is alive; the child can hang before `exec`, so the gate command never starts and the run cannot be terminated/recorded normally.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/kill_facts.py:_watching

chunk_findings.detail: `supported()` checks only that the current thread is the main thread, not that no other threads still have `CAPTURED` signals unblocked. If any pre-existing non-main thread is running with the default signal mask (for example a background metrics/logging thread), a process-directed `SIGTERM` can be delivered to that thread instead of being left pending. The watcher thread’s `sigtimedwait` will never see it; the fallback handler will raise and record the sender as `unknown`, even though the signal was sent in a supported Linux/main-thread environment and could otherwise have been named.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/kill_facts.py:supported

chunk_findings.detail: The wake-up path assumes `SIGUSR2` is unblocked in the main thread. `_watching` blocks only `CAPTURED` and later restores the old mask; it never unblocks `_SPAWN` (`SIGUSR2`). If the process is started with `SIGUSR2` blocked (the signal mask is inherited across `exec`), the watcher can consume a `SIGTERM`, call `pthread_kill(main_id, SIGUSR2)`, but the main thread cannot run `on_wake` while `SIGUSR2` remains blocked. The captured signal is removed from pending by `sigtimedwait`, yet the usual `RunTerminated` path is not woken, so the run may continue or the kill evidence may be delayed/lost until after the context exits.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/kill_facts.py:_watching

chunk_findings.detail: The kill-facts branch returns `lost_s` as `float(kill.get("lost_s") or 0.0)` without clamping negative values. A negative `lost_s` (possible from clock skew/race when `lost_s` is derived from elapsed/waited times, or from a malformed log entry) is summed and reported as negative lost work. For example, an event with `evidence={"kill": {"signal": "SIGTERM", "lost_s": -5}}` yields `lost_s=-5.0`; `build()` returns `"lost_s": -5.0`, and `text()` prints negative hours/minutes (“-0.0 h of work lost”, “-0.1 min lost”). The legacy negative-exit path explicitly clamps with `max(0.0, ...)`, so the kill-facts path is inconsistent and can produce impossible negative “work lost”.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/metrics/killed_runs.py:_facts_of

chunk_findings.detail: The gate command is built as a shell command string by interpolating `sys.executable` without shell quoting: `f"{sys.executable} -c \"...\"`. If the test Python lives at a path containing a space, such as `[REDACTED:path] Project/venv/bin/python`, the resulting command is parsed as an executable named `[REDACTED:path]` followed by extra arguments; the gate command never starts, `began` is never written, and `_start` fails after waiting 120 seconds. The same construction is also not robust to shell metacharacters or single quotes in the temporary path because Python `repr()` is not shell quoting.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_kill_facts.py:_setup

chunk_findings.detail: The review wrapper calls `_record_kill_facts(bound.arguments)` after `_begin_run()` but before `RUN.terminating(...)` has installed its signal mask/watcher. `_record_kill_facts` performs `Config.load(args["repo"])`, which can do filesystem I/O. If SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGINT is delivered while that config load is running (for example, a slow repo/config read or a `timeout` firing at that instant), the signal is still handled by the default disposition: the process dies before `RunTerminated` can be raised, so no `evidence.kill`/termination outcome is recorded even though `_begin_run()` has already forgotten prior run records. This new pre-mask I/O widens the signal race that the change is supposed to close.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/gate.py:_record_kill_facts wrapper

chunk_findings.detail: `signal.pthread_sigmask(signal.SIG_BLOCK, nums)` blocks SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGINT only in the current main thread. Existing threads that were started before `capturing` do not inherit that mask and remain eligible to receive a process-directed signal. If the run owner has any pre-existing thread (for example a log-reader or metrics thread) and the main thread is blocked in something like `subprocess.wait`, a SIGTERM sent to the owner can be delivered to that unblocked thread; the watcher thread’s `sigtimedwait` never returns and the main thread’s blocking syscall is not interrupted. The run then fails to terminate/record the kill, despite the docstring’s claim that signals delivered to non-blocking threads fall back to the plain handler.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/kill_facts.py:_watching

chunk_findings.detail: Nested uses of `capturing` can lose the captured signal. The outer watcher thread is still running when the inner `capturing` starts another watcher; both threads are blocked in `sigtimedwait` for the same signals. If the kernel delivers a SIGTERM to the outer watcher while the inner context is active, the outer watcher sends SIGUSR2 to the main thread, but the installed handler is the inner `on_wake`, which checks only the inner `pending` list, finds it empty, and returns. The wake-up is consumed and the outer watcher will not send another, so neither context raises `RunTerminated` and the kill facts are omitted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/kill_facts.py:_watching.on_wake

chunk_findings.detail: The wake-up signal SIGUSR2 is assumed to be deliverable, but `_watching` never unblocks it. If the run owner inherited a process/thread mask in which SIGUSR2 is blocked, `supported()` still returns true. When a captured SIGTERM arrives, the watcher consumes it with `sigtimedwait` and calls `signal.pthread_kill(main_id, SIGUSR2)`, but the main thread cannot receive SIGUSR2 because it is blocked. The final `signal.pthread_sigmask(signal.SIG_SETMASK, old_mask)` restores the same blocked SIGUSR2 mask, so the wake-up is never processed and the run is not terminated/recorded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/kill_facts.py:_watching

chunk_findings.detail: `sender_facts` treats any failure to read `/proc/<pid>/comm` as proof that the sender has exited. On a Linux system with `/proc` mounted with `hidepid=2` (or equivalent permission restrictions), a live sender from another user causes `_comm(pid)` to raise `PermissionError`, which is swallowed and returns `""`; `sender_facts` then records `sender: "exited"` and `sender_comm: "exited"` even though the sender is alive. For example, a root `timeout` process killing an unprivileged run would be misclassified as exited rather than unknown or named.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/kill_facts.py:sender_facts

chunk_findings.detail: `terminating` now starts a watcher thread via `kill_facts.capturing` whenever kill-fact recording is enabled, while gate children are launched from `adapters.proc` using `preexec_fn` to clear the inherited signal mask. Python’s `preexec_fn` is explicitly unsafe in a multithreaded process: after `fork`, other threads may hold locks, and the Python-level preexec function can deadlock before `exec`. A concrete case is a gate run with `[gates].record_kill_facts` enabled (the default in this function) where the command is started through `adapters.proc`: the watcher thread is alive, so the fork for the child can hang, making the run stall instead of launching. This is a regression from the old single-threaded signal-handler implementation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/running.py:terminating

chunk_findings.detail: `_facts_of` marks any `evidence.kill` with a truthy `signal` as `recorded=True` even when no sender was actually recorded: line 35 maps a missing/empty `sender_comm` to `"unknown"`, and line 36 maps a missing `sender_pid` to `0`. `build` then counts those rows in `with_sender_facts` (line 120), and `text` prints that count as “with sender facts”. For an outcome event with `evidence={"kill": {"signal": "SIGTERM", "lost_s": 60}}`, the report says “1 with sender facts” although the sender is unknown. This misstates the evidence used to decide kill causes; the count should require actual sender facts (e.g. a known `sender_pid`/`sender_comm`) or the field should be renamed to reflect that it counts only kill facts.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/metrics/killed_runs.py:39,120

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds a new `view=killed` metric and documents it, but the declared `view` parameter still validates against `choices=VIEWS`, and this diff does not add `"killed"` to `VIEWS`. Given input `ddflow metrics killed` (or an MCP call with `view="killed"`), parameter validation rejects the view before `service._own_fold` can handle it, making the new metrics view unreachable from the declared surface.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/metrics.py:Param("view").choices

chunk_findings.detail: `_setup` builds the gate command as a shell string and interpolates `sys.executable` without quoting it (`f"{sys.executable} -c ..."`). If the Python executable path contains spaces—e.g. a virtualenv under `[REDACTED:path] Project/venv/bin/python`—the stored command becomes `[REDACTED:path] Project/venv/bin/python -c ...`, which the shell or command splitter treats as an executable named `[REDACTED:path]` followed by arguments. The gate command then never starts, so `_start` times out and fails with “the gate command never started”.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_kill_facts.py:_setup

data.probe: capturing() installs fallback handlers for TERM/HUP/INT before blocking, so a signal delivered to a pre-existing unblocked thread raises RunTerminated in the main thread with sender recorded as unknown (never lost, never omitted). No ddflow gate/review owner thread exists before capturing() (CLI main thread only); the limitation is documented in the module docstring and help topic.

data.probe: CPython subprocess_fork_exec_impl calls PyOS_BeforeFork() when preexec_fn != None and PyOS_AfterFork_Child() in the child (Modules/_posixsubprocess.c, 3.13), and disables gc, precisely so Python code is safe in the child; the preexec is functools.partial(signal.pthread_sigmask, SIG_UNBLOCK, [...]), a single C call. Added only while the owner holds the signals blocked; measured: python3 -W error with a live thread + preexec_fn gave no warning and SigBlk 0 in the child (tests/test_gate_kill_facts.py::test_children_of_a_blocked_owner_start_with_the_signals_unblocked, test_the_gate_command_is_not_left_blocking_signals).
